summary.title: What is RCU? -- "Read, Copy, Update"
summary.one_liner: Learn the Linux kernel's RCU (Read-Copy-Update) synchronization model: split updates into removal and deferred reclamation, and use the five core APIs (rcu_read_lock/unlock, synchronize_rcu, call_rcu, rcu_assign_pointer, rcu_dereference).
takeaways: RCU splits an update into a removal phase (can run concurrently with readers) and a reclamation phase that waits until pre-existing readers finish.
The core API is small: rcu_read_lock(), rcu_read_unlock(), synchronize_rcu(), call_rcu(), rcu_assign_pointer() and rcu_dereference().
Readers use lightweight or no synchronization; updaters must still use locks to serialize concurrent writers.
Use synchronize_rcu() for simple blocking updates, or call_rcu()/kfree_rcu() when the updater cannot block.
A toy reader-writer-lock implementation of RCU illustrates the basic idea before the production kernel implementation in kernel/rcu/update.c.
summary.summary: This is the kernel's official RCU documentation, which explains the read-copy-update mechanism through several paths: a conceptual overview, an API walkthrough, example code protecting a global pointer, deferred updates with call_rcu(), toy implementations, and analogies to reader-writer locking and reference counting. It shows how readers enter and leave critical sections without heavy synchronization while updaters publish new versions and wait for a grace period before freeing old data. It also covers the rules for rcu_assign_pointer() and rcu_dereference() and notes the RCU flavors used in the kernel. The page links to the LWN series and other references for further reading.
